en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Bases (Āyatana-vibhaṅga) 1.
The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya)
The twelve sense bases:

the eye base, the form base, the ear base, the sound base, the nose base, the odor base, the tongue base, the taste base, the body base, the tangible-object base, the mind base, and the mental-phenomena base.
The eye is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
Forms are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
The ear is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
Sounds are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
The nose is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
Odors are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
The tongue is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
Tastes are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
The body is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
Tangible objects are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
The mind is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
Mental phenomena are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
This is the Analysis According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya).
2. Analysis According to the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya) The twelve bases (āyatana):

the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, the mind base; the visible-form base, the sound base, the odor base, the flavor base, the tangible-base, and the mental-object base.
In this context, what is the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*)?
It is that eye which, derived from the four great elements, is sensitive matter included within the personal organism, invisible and impinging;
by means of that invisible and impinging eye, one has seen, sees, or will see visible matter that is visible and impinging.
Whether one has seen, sees, or will see, this is the eye, this is the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), this is the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*),

this is the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*). This is the world, this is the door, this is the ocean, this is the white [lotus], this is the field, this is the site, this is the conduit, this is the guide,
this is the near shore, and this is the empty village.
This is called the "eye-base.
In this context, what is the "ear-base"?
It is that ear which, derived from the four great elements, is sensitive, included within the personal organism, invisible, and impinging.
That ear by which one has heard, hears, will hear, or is hearing a sound that is non-manifest and impinging—
this is the ear, this is the ear-base, this is the ear-element, this is the ear-faculty;
this is the world, this is the door, this is the ocean, this is the white [field], this is the field, this is the site, this is the hither shore, and this is the empty village.
This is called the "ear-base" (sotāyatana).
In this context, what is the "nose-base" (ghānāyatana)?
It is that nose which, derived from the four great elements, is sensitive matter included within the personal existence, invisible, and impinging.
That nose by which one has smelled, smells, will smell, or might smell an invisible and resistant odor— this is the nose, this is the nose-base,
this is the nose-element, this is the nose-faculty; this is the world, this is the door, this is the ocean, this is the white,
this is the field, this is the site, this is the hither shore, this is the empty village.
This is called the nose-base (*ghānāyatana*).
In this context, what is the tongue-base (*jivhāyatana*)?
It is that which is the tongue—the sensitive matter derived from the four great elements, included within the personal organism, invisible, and impinging.
That tongue which is non-manifest and impinging, by which one has tasted, tastes, will taste, or might taste a flavor that is non-manifest and impinging—
this is the tongue, this is the tongue-base, this is the tongue-element, this is the faculty of the tongue.
This is the world, this is the door, this is the ocean, this is the white [lotus], this is the field, this is the site, this is the hither shore, and this is the empty village.
This is called the tongue-base (*jivhāyatana*).
In this context, what is the body-base (*kāyāyatana*)?
It is that sensitive matter derived from the four great elements which is included within the personal organism, invisible, and impinging.
That body which, being invisible and possessing resistance, has touched, touches, will touch, or touches the invisible and resistant tangible object—
this is the body, this is the body-base, this is the body-element, this is the body-faculty; this is the world, this is the door, this is the ocean, this is the white [cloth],
this is the field, this is the site, this is the hither shore, this is the empty village.
This is called the "base of the body.
In that regard, what is the "base of the mind"?
The base of the mind is of one kind.
Associated with contact.
The mind base is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The mind-base is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate.
The mind-base is fourfold:
There is that pertaining to the sense-sphere, there is that pertaining to the fine-material sphere, there is that pertaining to the immaterial sphere, and there is that which is non-included.
The mind-base is fivefold:

there is that associated with the faculty of pleasure, there is that associated with the faculty of pain, there is that associated with the faculty of mental joy, there is that associated with the faculty of mental grief, and there is that associated with the faculty of equanimity.
The mind-base is sixfold:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
Thus is the mind-base sixfold.
The mind-base is sevenfold:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element.
Thus is the mind-base sevenfold.
The mind-base is eightfold:

eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness (which is accompanied by pleasure, and which is accompanied by pain), the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element.
Thus is the mind-base eightfold.
The mind-base is ninefold:

eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—which may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Thus is the mind-base ninefold.
The mind-base is tenfold: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness— which is accompanied by pleasure,
which is accompanied by pain— the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element— which is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Thus is the sense base of mind by way of tenfold classification.
By way of a singlefold classification, the sense base of mind is that which is associated with contact.
The mind-base is twofold:

there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause. The mind-base is threefold: [it is associated with pleasure, associated with pain, and associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure].

There is that associated with pleasant feeling, there is that associated with painful feeling, and there is that associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling … [and so on] … Thus is the sense base of mind (manāyatana) of many kinds.
This is called “the sense base of mind.”
In this context, what is the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*)?
It is that form which, derived from the four great elements, possesses color and luster, is visible, and offers resistance;
namely: blue, yellow, red, white, black, crimson, green, the color of a parrot, the color of a mango sprout, long...
Short, minute, large, round, circular, square, hexagonal, octagonal, sixteen-sided;
low, high, shadow, heat, light, darkness, cloud, mist, smoke, dust;
the appearance and color of the moon’s disk, the appearance and color of the sun’s disk, the appearance and color of the stars, and the appearance and color of a mirror’s disk.
The appearance of gems, conch shells, pearls, beryl, gold, and silver;
or whatever other form there is that is a derivative of the four great elements, appearing as color, visible and impinging—
whatever such form, visible and impinging, one has seen, sees, or will see with the eye, which is invisible and impinging.
Or what has been seen, or will be seen, or is being seen—this is form, this is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), this is the element of form (*rūpadhātu*).
This is called the "sense-sphere of form.
In that regard, what is the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*)?
Whatever sound there is derived from the four great elements— non-manifest and impinging— such as the sound of a drum, the sound of a kettledrum, the sound of a conch,

the sound of a tambourine, the sound of singing, the sound of instrumental music, the sound of clapping, the sound of hand-clapping, the vocal sounds of beings, the sounds of the collision of elements,
the sound of wind, the sound of water, the sound of humans, the sound of non-humans, or whatever other [sound there may be].
There is sound derived from the four great elements that is non-manifest and impinging; that sound which is non-manifest and impinging—
one has heard, hears, will hear, or is hearing with the ear that is non-manifest and impinging—
this is sound, this is the sound-base (*saddāyatana*), this is the sound-element (*saddhadhātu*).
This is called the sense-sphere of sound.
In this context, what is the sense-sphere of odor?
It is that odor derived from the four great elements which is invisible and impingent, such as the odor of roots, the odor of heartwood, and so forth.
The scent of roots, the scent of leaves, the scent of flowers, the scent of fruits, the scent of raw flesh, the foul scent, the pleasant scent, the unpleasant scent,
or whatever other scent there is that is derived from the four great elements,
invisible and impinging— any such scent that is invisible and impinging which one has smelled, smells, or will smell with the nose, which is itself invisible and impinging.
Or it will be smelled, or it is being smelled; this is odor, this is the odor base (*gandhāyatana*), this is the odor element (*gandhadhātu*).
This is called "the odor base.
In that regard, what is the taste base (*rasāyatana*)?

Whatever taste there is derived from the four great elements—whether invisible and impinging, or the taste of roots, the taste of trunks, the taste of bark, the taste of leaves, the taste of flowers, or the taste of fruits;
whether sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, astringent, or acrid;
whether savory or insipid; or whatever other taste there may be derived from the four great elements.

Depending on [the tongue], that which is invisible and impinging, the taste which is invisible and impinging, whether one has tasted, tastes, will taste, or is tasting it with the invisible and impinging tongue—
this is taste, this is the sense-sphere of taste (*rasāyatana*), this is the element of taste (*rasadhātu*).
This is called "the sense-sphere of taste."
In this context, what is the sense-sphere of the tangible?

It is the earth element, the fire element, and the air element; hardness, softness, smoothness, roughness, pleasant contact, painful contact, heaviness, and lightness—whatever tangible object is invisible and impinging, [to be experienced] by the body.
Whether it has touched, touches, will touch, or touches by means of that which is non-indicative and impinging—
this is tangibility, this is the tangibility base, this is the tangibility element.
This is called the "tangibility base."
Therein, what is the sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana)?

It is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, that form which is non-manifesting and non-reactive and is included within the sphere of mental phenomena, and the unconditioned element.
Therein, what is the aggregate of feeling?
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which has a cause; there is that which is without a cause.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate …pe…
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division; ... [and so on] ...
thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of manifold division.
This is called "the aggregate of feeling."
Therein, what is the aggregate of perception?
The aggregate of perception is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of perception is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The aggregate of perception is threefold:
There is wholesome, there is unwholesome, there is indeterminate … [and so on] … thus is the aggregate of perception tenfold;
… thus is the aggregate of perception manifold.
This is called the aggregate of perception.
In this context, what is the aggregate of mental formations?
The aggregate of mental formations is of one kind:
Associated with consciousness.
The aggregate of mental formations is twofold:
there is that which is a root-cause, and there is that which is not a root-cause.
The aggregate of mental formations is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate … [and so on] … thus the aggregate of mental formations is tenfold … [and so on].
In this way, the aggregate of formations is of many kinds.
This is called the "aggregate of formations.
In that regard, what is form that is non-manifesting, non-reactive, and included within the sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana)?
The femininity faculty, the masculinity faculty … [and so on] … edible food.
This is called form that is "invisible and non-reacting, included within the sphere of mental phenomena" (dhammāyatana).
In this context, what is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)?
The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—
this is called the unconditioned element.
This is called the sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana).
The Exposition of the Abhidhamma.
3. The Interrogation by Questions.
The twelve bases:
The eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, the tangible-base, the mind-base, and the mental-object-base.
Of these twelve bases, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate? …pe… How many are with conflict, and how many are without conflict? 3.1.
The Triads.
Ten bases are indeterminate.
Two bases may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate.
Ten bases are not to be described as [wholesome or unwholesome].
“Associated with pleasant feeling,” or “associated with painful feeling,” or “associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The sense base of the mind may be associated with pleasant feeling, may be associated with painful feeling, or may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The sense base of mental phenomena may be associated with pleasant feeling, may be associated with painful feeling, [or may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling].

It may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; it may be such that it cannot be said to be "associated with pleasant feeling," nor "associated with painful feeling," nor even "associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Ten bases are neither resultant nor subject to resultancy.
Two bases may be resultant, may be subject to result, or may be neither-resultant-nor-subject-to-result.
Five bases are acquired and subject to clinging.
The sound base is not acquired but is subject to clinging.
Four bases may be both acquired and subject to clinging, may be unacquired but subject to clinging, or may be neither subject to clinging nor acquired.
Two bases may be both acquired and subject to clinging, may be unacquired but subject to clinging, or may be neither acquired nor subject to clinging.
Ten bases are neither defiled nor subject to defilement.
Two bases may be defiled and subject to defilement; they may be undefiled but subject to defilement; they may be undefiled and not subject to defilement.
Ten bases are without initial application and without sustained application.

The mind base may be with initial application and sustained application; it may be without initial application and with sustained application only; it may be without initial application and without sustained application.

The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be with applied thought and sustained thought, may be without applied thought and with sustained thought only, or may be without applied thought and without sustained thought; it may also not be described as "with applied thought and sustained thought," nor as "without applied thought and with sustained thought only," nor as "without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Ten spheres (āyatana) are not to be so described.
They are either accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*), or accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*), or accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*).

Two bases may be accompanied by rapture, may be accompanied by pleasure, may be accompanied by equanimity, or they may not be described as being "accompanied by rapture," "accompanied by pleasure," or "accompanied by equanimity.
Ten bases are not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
Two bases may be abandonable by vision, may be abandonable by cultivation, or may be neither abandonable by vision nor abandonable by cultivation.
Ten bases have roots that are neither abandonable by vision nor abandonable by cultivation.

Two bases may have roots that are not abandonable by vision, may have roots that are abandonable by cultivation, or may have roots that are neither abandonable by vision nor abandonable by cultivation.
Ten bases neither lead to accumulation nor lead to diminution.
Two bases may lead to accumulation, may lead to diminution, or may neither lead to accumulation nor lead to diminution.
Ten bases are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Two bases may be of those in training (sekha), may be of those beyond training (asekha), or may be neither of those in training nor beyond training.
Ten bases are limited (paritta).
Two bases may be limited, may be exalted (mahaggata), or may be immeasurable (appamāṇa).
Ten bases have no objects.
Two bases may have limited objects, may have exalted objects, may have immeasurable objects, or may not be described as having "limited objects," "exalted objects," or "immeasurable objects.
Ten bases are intermediate.
Two bases may be inferior, may be middling, or may be superior.
Ten bases are indeterminate.
Two bases may be fixed in the wrongness, may be fixed in the rightness, or may be indeterminate.
Ten bases are without an object.

Two bases may have the Path as their object, may have the Path as their cause, or may have the Path as their predominance; or they may not be described as having the Path as their object, nor as having the Path as their cause, nor as having the Path as their predominance.
Five bases may be arisen, or may be bound to arise; they are not to be described [otherwise].
“Unarisen”: the sense-sphere of sound may be arisen, it may be unarisen, but it should not be said that it “will arise.”
The five sense bases may be arisen, may be unarisen, or may be bound to arise.
The base of mental phenomena may be arisen, may be unarisen, or may be bound to arise; it should not be said to be either "arisen," "unarisen," or "bound to arise.
Eleven bases may be past, may be future, or may be present.
The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be past, may be future, may be present, or it may not be described as "past," "future," or "present.
Ten spheres have no object.
Two spheres may have a past object, may have a future object, may have a present object, or they may not be described as having a "past object," "future object," or "present object."
They may be internal, they may be external, or they may be both internal and external.
Ten bases have no object.

Two bases may have an internal object, may have an external object, or may have an internal-external object; or they may not be described as having an internal object, nor as having an external object, nor as having an internal-external object.
The sphere of visible form is with visibility and with resistance.
Nine spheres are without visibility but with resistance.
Two spheres are without visibility and without resistance.
Hetugocchaka:
Eleven bases are not roots.
The sphere of mental phenomena may be a cause, or it may not be a cause.
Ten spheres are without cause.
Two spheres may be with cause, or they may be without cause.
Ten bases are dissociated from roots.
Two bases may be associated with roots, or they may be dissociated from roots.
Ten bases should not be said [to be either].

[The mind-base] may be both a cause and accompanied by a cause; it may also be accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause. The mind-base should not be said to be "both a cause and accompanied by a cause";
it may be accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause, or it may not be said to be "accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause."

The sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana) may be both a cause and accompanied by a cause; it may be accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause; it may be neither "both a cause and accompanied by a cause" nor "accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause.
Ten spheres (āyatana) should not be described as either "both causes and associated with causes" or "associated with causes but not themselves causes."

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) should not be said to be "both a cause and associated with a cause"; it may be associated with a cause but not itself a cause, or it may not be said to be "associated with a cause but not itself a cause.

The mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*) may be both a cause and associated with a cause; it may be associated with a cause but not itself a cause; or it may not be said to be either "both a cause and associated with a cause" or "associated with a cause but not itself a cause."
Ten bases are neither-root-conditions nor rootless.
The mind base may be not-root-conditioned-with-root, or it may be neither-root-condition nor rootless.

The mental-object base may be not-root-conditioned-with-root, or it may be neither-root-condition nor rootless, or it may be such that it should not be said to be either "not-root-conditioned-with-root" or "neither-root-condition nor rootless."
3.2.2. The Minor Intermediate Dyads Eleven bases are with conditions.
The base of mental phenomena may be with conditions, or it may be without conditions.
Eleven bases are conditioned.
The base of mental phenomena may be conditioned or unconditioned.
The base of visible forms is with visibility.
Eleven bases are non-demonstrable.
Ten bases are impinging.
Two bases are non-impinging.
Ten bases are material.
The mind base is immaterial.
The mental-object base may be material or it may be immaterial.
Ten bases are mundane.
Two bases may be either mundane or supramundane;
they may be cognizable by some [consciousness] and not cognizable by others.
3.2.3. The Group on the Taints (Āsava-gocchaka).
Eleven bases are not taints.
The base of mental phenomena may be a taint, or it may not be a taint.
Ten bases are associated with the taints.
Two bases may be either associated with the taints or dissociated from the taints.
Ten bases are dissociated from the taints.
Two bases may be associated with the taints (*āsava*),
and they may be dissociated from the taints. Ten bases should not be described as "both taints and tainted (*sāsava*)," but rather as "tainted but not taints."
The mind base (*manāyatana*) should not be said to be "both a taint (*āsava*) and tainted (*sāsava*"); it may be tainted but not a taint, or it may not be said to be "tainted but not a taint.
The mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) may be both a taint and tainted, it may be tainted but not a taint, or it may not be said to be either "both a taint and tainted" or "tainted but not a taint."
The ten bases should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints.
The mind base should not be so described.

Regarding the phrase “both an outflow (āsava) and associated with an outflow”: it may be associated with an outflow but not itself an outflow; it may be such that it cannot be said to be “both an outflow and associated with an outflow”;

and it may be such that it cannot be said to be either “both an outflow and associated with an outflow” or “associated with an outflow but not itself an outflow. The sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana) may be both an outflow and associated with an outflow;

it may be associated with an outflow but not itself an outflow; and it may be such that it cannot be said to be either “both an outflow and associated with an outflow” or “associated with an outflow but not itself an outflow.”
Ten bases are dissociated from the taints and are subject to taints.

Two bases may be dissociated from the taints and subject to taints, may be dissociated from the taints and not subject to taints, or may not be described as either "dissociated from the taints and subject to taints" or "dissociated from the taints and not subject to taints.
3.2.4. The Group on the Fetters (Saṃyojana-gocchaka)
Eleven bases are not fetters.
The base of mental phenomena may be a fetter, and may not be a fetter.
Ten bases are objects of the fetters.
Two bases may be subject to the fetters; they may be not subject to the fetters.
Ten bases are dissociated from the fetters.
Two bases may be associated with the fetters; they may be dissociated from the fetters.
The ten bases should not be described as "both fetters and objects of fettering," but rather as "objects of fettering but not fetters.
The mind base should not be described [in that way].

Regarding the phrase “both a fetter and the object of a fetter”: it may be the object of a fetter but not itself a fetter; it may be such that it cannot be said to be “the object of a fetter but not itself a fetter.
The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be both a fetter and the object of a fetter; it may be the object of a fetter but not itself a fetter;
and it may be such that it cannot be said to be either “a fetter and the object of a fetter” or “the object of a fetter but not itself a fetter.”
The ten bases should not be described as "both fetters and associated with fetters," nor as "associated with fetters but not fetters.
The mind base should not be so described.

Regarding the phrase “both a fetter and associated with a fetter”: it may be associated with a fetter but not itself a fetter; it may be such that it cannot be said to be “both a fetter and associated with a fetter.
The sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana) may be both a fetter and associated with a fetter; it may be associated with a fetter but not itself a fetter;
and it may be such that it cannot be said to be “both a fetter and associated with a fetter.”
“Associated with the fetters but not being a fetter itself.
Ten bases are dissociated from the fetters and are objects of the fetters (*saṃyojaniya*).

Two bases may be dissociated from the fetters and objects of the fetters; they may be dissociated from the fetters and not objects of the fetters; or they may not be described as either “dissociated from the fetters and objects of the fetters” or “dissociated from the fetters and not objects of the fetters.”
3.2.5. The Group on the Fetter (Ganthagocchaka) Eleven bases are not fetters.
The base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be a fetter, or it may not be a fetter.
Ten bases are objects of the ties.
Two bases may be objects of the ties, or they may not be objects of the ties.
Ten bases are dissociated from the ties.
Two bases may be associated with the fetters, or they may be dissociated from the fetters.
Ten bases should not be said to be "both fetters and objects of the fetters"; rather, they are objects of the fetters but are not themselves fetters.

The sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) should not be said to be "both a tie (*gantha*) and a thing to be tied (*ganthaniya*"); it may be a thing to be tied but not a tie, or it may not be said to be "a thing to be tied but not a tie.

The sense-base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) may be both a tie and a thing to be tied, it may be a thing to be tied but not a tie, or it may not be said to be either "both a tie and a thing to be tied" or "a thing to be tied but not a tie."
The ten bases (dasāyatana) should not be described as "both fetters and associated with fetters," nor as "associated with fetters but not fetters.
The mind base (manāyatana) should not be described [in either way].

Regarding the phrase “both a tie (*gantha*) and associated with a tie (*ganthasampayutta*”), it may be associated with a tie but not a tie itself; it may not be said that “it is associated with a tie but not a tie.
The sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) may be both a tie and associated with a tie; it may be associated with a tie but not a tie;
and it may not be said either that “it is both a tie and associated with a tie” or that “it is associated with a tie but not a tie.”
Ten bases (āyatana) are dissociated from the fetters (gantha) and are subject to the fetters.

Two bases may be dissociated from the fetters and subject to the fetters; they may be dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters; or they may not be described as either "dissociated from the fetters and subject to the fetters" or "dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters.
2.3.2.6. The Group on Floods (ogha), Yokes (yoga), and Hindrances (nīvaraṇa)
The eleven bases are not floods … [and so on] … not yokes … [and so on] … not hindrances.
The sphere of mental phenomena may be an hindrance, or it may not be an hindrance.
Ten spheres are conducive to hindrances.
Two spheres may be conducive to hindrances, or they may not be conducive to hindrances.
Ten bases are dissociated from the hindrances.
Two bases may be associated with the hindrances, or they may be dissociated from the hindrances. Ten bases should not be said to be [associated with the hindrances].
Regarding the phrase “both hindrances and conducive to hindrance”: there are things that are conducive to hindrance but are not themselves hindrances.

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) should not be said to be “both a hindrance and conducive to hindrance”; it may be conducive to hindrance but not itself a hindrance, or it may not be said to be “conducive to hindrance but not itself a hindrance.”

The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be both an obscuration (nīvaraṇa) and conducive to obscurations (nīvaraṇiya); it may be conducive to obscurations but not itself an obscuration; or it may be such that it cannot be said to be "both an obscuration and conducive to obscurations," nor can it be said to be "conducive to obscurations but not itself an obscuration.
Ten bases (āyatana) cannot be said to be "both obscurations and associated with obscurations," nor can they be said to be "associated with obscurations but not themselves obscurations."

The mind-base (manāyatana) should not be said to be "both an hindrance and associated with an hindrance"; it may be associated with an hindrance but not itself an hindrance, or it may not be said to be "associated with an hindrance but not itself an hindrance.
The mental-object-base (dhammāyatana) may be both an hindrance and associated with an hindrance, or it may be associated with an hindrance... [and so forth].

And that which is not an hindrance may be such that it cannot be said to be "both an hindrance and associated with an hindrance," nor can it be said to be "associated with an hindrance but not an hindrance.
Ten bases are dissociated from hindrances and are objects of hindrance.

Two bases may be dissociated from the hindrances but subject to them; they may be dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to them; or they may not be described as either "dissociated from the hindrances but subject to them" or "dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to them.
3.2.9. The Group on Misapprehension (Parāmāsa-gocchaka):
Eleven bases are not misapprehensions.
The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be an object of clinging (parāmāsa), or it may not be an object of clinging.
Ten spheres are objects of clinging.
Two spheres may be objects of clinging, or they may not be objects of clinging.
Ten bases are dissociated from the perversions.
The mind base may be associated with the perversions, or it may be dissociated from the perversions.

The mental-object base may be associated with the perversions, or it may be dissociated from the perversions, or it should not be said to be either "associated with the perversions" or "dissociated from the perversions."
The ten bases (dasāyatana) should not be described as "both corruptions (parāmāsa) and corrupted (parāmaṭṭha)," nor as "corrupted but not corruptions.
The mind-base (manāyatana) should not be described [in either way].

Regarding the phrase “both a misapprehension and that which is misapprehended”: there may be something that is misapprehended but is not a misapprehension; there may be something that should not be described as “both a misapprehension and that which is misapprehended.

The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be both a misapprehension and that which is misapprehended; it may be that which is misapprehended but is not a misapprehension; and it may be neither “a misapprehension and that which is misapprehended” nor “that which is misapprehended but is not a misapprehension.
The ten sense-bases (dasāyatana) are dissociated from misapprehension and are misapprehended.

Two bases may be dissociated from the taints and associated with misapprehension; they may be dissociated from the taints and not associated with misapprehension; or they may be so designated as neither "dissociated from the taints and associated with misapprehension" nor "dissociated from the taints and not associated with misapprehension.
3.2.10. The Decad of Greatness:
Ten bases are without an object.
The mind-base has an object.
The mental-object-base may have an object, or it may be without an object.
The mind-base is consciousness.
Eleven bases are not mind.
Eleven bases are not mental factors.
The base of mental phenomena may be a mental factor, or it may not be a mental factor.
Ten bases are dissociated from consciousness.
The base of mental phenomena may be associated with consciousness, or it may be dissociated from consciousness.
The mind base is not to be described [in this way].
“Associated with consciousness,” and also “dissociated from consciousness.
Ten bases are dissociated from consciousness.
The base of mental phenomena may be associated with consciousness, and may be dissociated from consciousness.
The mind-base (manāyatana) should not be said to be "conjoined with consciousness" nor "disjoined from consciousness.
The six bases are not originated by consciousness.
The six bases may be mind-originated, or they may not be mind-originated.
Eleven bases do not coexist with the mind.
The base of mental phenomena may coexist with the mind, or it may not coexist with the mind.
Eleven bases do not follow the mind.
The base of mental phenomena may follow the mind, or it may not follow the mind.
Eleven bases are neither conjoined with nor produced by the mind.
The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be conjoined with and produced by consciousness, or it may not be conjoined with and produced by consciousness.
Eleven spheres are neither conjoined with, nor produced by, nor co-existent with consciousness.
The sphere of mental phenomena may be conjoined with, produced by, and co-existent with consciousness, or it may not be conjoined with, produced by, or co-existent with consciousness.
Eleven bases are not conjoined with, originated by, and concomitant with consciousness.
The base of mental phenomena may be conjoined with, originated by, and concomitant with consciousness, or it may not be conjoined with, originated by, and concomitant with consciousness.
Six bases are internal.
Six bases are external.
Nine bases are derived.
Two bases are not derived.
The sphere of mental phenomena may be derived, or it may not be derived.
The five spheres [of sense] are derived.
The sphere of sounds is not derived.
The six bases may be clung-to, or they may not be clung-to.
3.2.11. Group on Clinging:
Eleven bases are not clinging.
The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be subject to clinging (upādāna), or it may not be subject to clinging.
Ten spheres are subject to clinging.
Two spheres may be subject to clinging, or they may not be subject to clinging.
Ten bases are dissociated from clinging.
Two bases may be associated with clinging, or they may be dissociated from clinging.
Ten bases should not be said [to be either].
Regarding the phrase “both clinging and objects of clinging”: there are things that are objects of clinging but are not themselves clinging.

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) should not be said to be “both clinging and an object of clinging”; it may be an object of clinging but not itself clinging, or it may not be said to be “an object of clinging but not itself clinging.”

The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be both clinging (*upādāna*) and subject to clinging (*upādāniya*); it may be subject to clinging but not clinging; or it may be neither "clinging and subject to clinging" nor "subject to clinging but not clinging.
Ten spheres cannot be described as either "both clinging and associated with clinging" or "associated with clinging but not clinging."

The sense-base of mind (manāyatana) should not be said to be "both subject to clinging and associated with clinging"; it may be associated with clinging but not itself clinging, or it may not be said to be "associated with clinging but not itself clinging.
The sense-base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be both clinging and associated with clinging, or it may be associated with clinging [but not itself clinging].
And there is nothing that is clinging which should be described as "both clinging and associated with clinging," nor as "associated with clinging but not clinging.
Ten bases are dissociated from clinging and are objects of clinging.

Two bases may be associated with clinging and subject to clinging; they may be dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging; or they may be so that it cannot be said whether they are "dissociated from clinging and subject to clinging" or "dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging.
3.2.12. The Group on Defilements:
Eleven bases are not defilements.
The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be an affliction (kilesa), or it may not be an affliction.
Ten spheres are subject to affliction (saṅkilesika).
Two spheres may be subject to affliction, or they may not be subject to affliction.
Ten bases are undefiled.
Two bases may be defiled, or they may be undefiled.
Ten bases are dissociated from the defilements.
Two bases may be associated with defilements; they may be dissociated from defilements.
Ten bases should not be said to be "both defilements and objects of defilement"; rather, they are objects of defilement but not themselves defilements.
The mind-base (*manāyatana*) should not be said to be "both a defilement and defiled"; it may be defiled but not a defilement, or it may not be said to be "defiled but not a defilement.

The mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*) may be both a defilement and defiled; it may be defiled but not a defilement; or it may not be said to be either "both a defilement and defiled" or "defiled but not a defilement."
The ten bases (dasāyatana) should not be described as "both defilements and defiled," nor as "defiled but not defilements.
The mind base (manāyatana) should not be so described.

“Both an affliction (*kilesa*) and defiled (*saṅkiliṭṭha*): it may be that something is defiled but not an affliction; it may be that something cannot be said to be “both an affliction and defiled,” nor can it be said to be “defiled but not an affliction.

The sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) may be both an affliction and defiled; it may be defiled but not an affliction; it may be that neither can be said—that it is “both an affliction and defiled,” nor that it is “defiled but not an affliction.
Ten spheres (*dasāyatana*) cannot be so described.
[The mind-object base] may be both a defilement and associated with defilements; it may also be associated with defilements but not itself a defilement.

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) should not be said to be both a defilement and associated with defilements; it may be associated with defilements but not itself a defilement, or it may not be said to be associated with defilements but not itself a defilement.
The sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be both a defilement and associated with defilements; it may be associated with defilements but not itself a defilement;
and it may be such that it cannot be said to be "both a defilement and associated with defilements," nor can it be said to be "associated with defilements but not itself a defilement.
Ten spheres are dissociated from defilements yet are subject to defilement (saṅkilesika).

Two bases may be dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement; they may be dissociated from the defilements and not subject to defilement; or they may be so that it cannot be said whether they are "dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement" or "dissociated from the defilements and not subject to defilement.
3.2.13. The Subsequent Pair:
Ten bases are not to be abandoned by seeing.
Two bases may be abandoned by vision, or they may not be abandoned by vision.
Ten bases are not to be abandoned by cultivation.
Two bases may be abandoned by cultivation, or they may not be abandoned by cultivation.
Ten bases do not have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.
Two bases may have roots that are to be abandoned by vision, and may have roots that are not to be abandoned by vision.
Ten bases do not have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Two bases may have roots to be abandoned by cultivation, or they may not have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
Ten bases are without applied thought.
Two bases may be with applied thought, or they may be without applied thought.
Ten bases are without investigation.
Two bases may be with investigation, or they may be without investigation.
Ten bases are without rapture.
Two bases may be accompanied by rapture; they may be without rapture. Ten bases are not associated with rapture.
Two bases may be associated with rapture; they may not be associated with rapture.
Ten bases are not accompanied by pleasure.
Two bases may be accompanied by pleasure, or they may not be accompanied by pleasure.
Ten bases are not accompanied by equanimity.
Two bases may be accompanied by equanimity, or they may not be accompanied by equanimity.
Ten bases belong to the sense-sphere.
Two bases may belong to the sense-sphere, or they may not belong to the sense-sphere.
Ten bases are not of the fine-material sphere.
Two bases may be of the fine-material sphere, or they may not be of the fine-material sphere.
Ten bases are not of the immaterial sphere.
Two bases may be formless-sphere (arūpāvacara), or they may not be formless-sphere.
Ten bases are included (pariyāpanna).
Two bases may be included, or they may be unincluded (apariyāpanna).
Ten bases are not conducive to liberation.
Two bases may be conducive to liberation, or they may not be conducive to liberation.
Ten bases are indeterminate.
Two bases may be determinate; they may be indeterminate.
Ten bases are surpassable.
Two bases may be surpassable; they may be unsurpassable.
Ten bases are without conflict (*araṇa*).
Two bases may be with conflict (*saraṇa*) or may be without conflict.
This is the section of questions and answers.
The Analysis of the Bases is finished.
